function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

message.content:
When you need to store and query currency valuations (exchange rates) over time, the goal is usually to: 1. **Keep the data compact** – exchange rates change only a few times per day, so you don’t need a record for every second. 2. **Support fast look‑ups** – you often want “what was the rate on this date?” or “what was the rate at this timestamp?” 3. **Allow efficient range queries** – e.g., “give me all rates between Jan 1 and Jan 10.” 4. **Handle updates** – new rates arrive daily, sometimes with corrections. A combination of a **time‑series database** and a **columnar storage** model is typically the most effective. Below are the top options and why they work well. --- ## 1. Time‑Series Database (TSDB) | TSDB | Why it’s great for currency rates | |------|------------------------------------| | **InfluxDB** | • Built‑in retention policies (e.g., keep 1 year of data, downsample older data).
• Continuous queries for automatic downsampling.
• High write throughput (hundreds of writes per second). | | **TimescaleDB** (PostgreSQL extension) | • Full SQL support + powerful extensions (e.g., `timescaledb_experimental`).
• Hypertables automatically partition by time.
• Seamless integration with existing PostgreSQL tooling. | | **Prometheus** | • Simple key/value model; great for metrics.
• Retention policies & downsampling via remote write.
• Excellent for real‑time monitoring dashboards. | | **OpenTSDB** | • Scales horizontally across many nodes.
• Uses HBase/HDFS for storage; good for very large datasets. | ### Typical schema ```sql -- TimescaleDB example CREATE TABLE currency_rates ( ts TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, base TEXT NOT NULL, -- e.g., "USD" quote TEXT NOT NULL, -- e.g., "EUR" rate DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (ts, base, quote) ); SELECT create_hypertable('currency_rates', 'ts'); ``` ### Advantages - **Retention & downsampling**: Keep raw data for the last 90 days, then aggregate to hourly/daily averages for older periods. - **Indexing**: Primary key on `(ts, base, quote)` gives O(log n) look‑ups. - **Query language**: SQL or InfluxQL/Flux lets you do complex aggregations (`AVG`, `MAX`, `MIN`) over arbitrary windows. - **Scalability**: Horizontal scaling (sharding) is built‑in for TimescaleDB; InfluxDB clusters can handle millions of points per second. --- ## 2. Columnar Storage (e.g., Parquet + Delta Lake) If you prefer a data lake approach (e.g., for analytics pipelines), store each day’s rates as a Parquet file in a Delta Lake table. | Tool | Why it’s useful | |------|-----------------| | **Delta Lake** | • ACID transactions on top of Parquet.
• Time travel & versioning.
• Schema evolution. | | **Parquet** | • Columnar format → very efficient compression & query performance.
• Works with Spark, Hive, Presto, Trino. | ### Typical layout ``` /data/currency_rates/ ├── year=2024/month=01/day=01/ │ └── part-00000.parquet ├── year=2024/month=01/day=02/ │ └── part-00000.parquet ... ``` ### Advantages - **Batch analytics**: Spark jobs can read only the relevant partitions (e.g., `WHERE year=2024 AND month=01`). - **Cost‑effective**: Store older data in cheaper storage tiers (e.g., S3 Glacier). - **Versioning**: Keep a history of corrections or re‑calculations. --- ## 3. Hybrid Approach Many production systems combine both: 1. **Ingest** new rates into a TSDB for real‑time access. 2. **Periodically** snapshot the TSDB into a Delta Lake table for long‑term analytics. 3. **Delete** raw TSDB data older than the retention window (e.g., 90 days). This gives you the best of both worlds: low‑latency queries for recent data and cost‑efficient storage for historical data. --- ## 4. In‑Memory Cache (Optional) For ultra‑low latency (e.g., high‑frequency trading), keep the most recent 24 hours in an in‑memory cache (Redis, Memcached, or even a local LRU cache). The cache can be refreshed from the TSDB every few minutes. --- ## 5. Choosing the Right Tool | Scenario | Recommended TSDB | Recommended Columnar | |----------|------------------|----------------------| | **Real‑time dashboards** | InfluxDB (or TimescaleDB) | — | | **Historical analytics** | — | Delta Lake + Parquet | | **Hybrid** | TimescaleDB | Delta Lake | | **Very large scale (millions of points/day)** | OpenTSDB | — | --- ## 6. Quick Implementation Sketch ```bash # 1. Set up TimescaleDB docker run -d --name timescaledb -p 5432:5432 timescale/timescaledb:latest-pg13 # 2. Create hypertable psql -h localhost -U postgres <<'SQL' CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS timescaledb; CREATE TABLE currency_rates ( ts TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, base TEXT NOT NULL, quote TEXT NOT NULL, rate DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (ts, base, quote) ); SELECT create_hypertable('currency_rates', 'ts'); SQL # 3. Insert sample data psql -h localhost -U postgres <<'SQL' INSERT INTO currency_rates VALUES ('2024-05-31 12:00:00+00', 'USD', 'EUR', 0.92), ('2024-05-31 12:00:00+00', 'USD', 'JPY', 140.5); SQL # 4. Query psql -h localhost -U postgres <<'SQL' SELECT * FROM currency_rates WHERE ts >= '2024-05-01' AND ts < '2024-06-01' ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 10; SQL ``` --- ## Bottom Line - **For real‑time access + retention**: Use a TSDB (TimescaleDB or InfluxDB). - **For batch analytics + long‑term storage**: Store snapshots in a columnar format (Delta Lake + Parquet). - **For the best of both**: Keep a hybrid pipeline that writes to the TSDB for the last 90 days and periodically snapshots into the data lake. This architecture scales horizontally, keeps costs low, and gives you fast, flexible queries for currency valuations over time.
